description: We’re Rishab and Kabir, high school students from Shrewsbury, Massachusettsand we love programming and developing innovative solutions to problems. We both write SwiftUI and React and have been building for a year or two. Kabir has four apps on the App Store and has been coding since he was 7. Rishab is building Anchor, an AI tool for teachers. For Space Apps we built Southlight, a tool that lets anyone pick a date and see which south-pole landing sites get sunlight and a line of sight to Earth.
summary:
Southlight is a browser-based navigator for the Moon's south pole. Pick a date between 2026 and 2030 and see, for three south-pole sites from NASA's Artemis III candidate-region lists, whether a lander would have sunlight and a clear line of sight to Earth, summed up as a Good, Risky or Poor verdict.

It addresses the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by turning specialist orbital and terrain analysis into one view that mission planners, teachers and the public can all read. The Sun and Earth move to their real positions around the Moon, a skyline chart shows them against the local horizon, and one click finds a better window.

It matters because at the south pole the Sun stays close to the horizon, so local terrain decides whether a lander stays powered and connected. A site that looks fine on one date can be dark, or out of contact, on another.

Everything is built from NASA SPICE ephemerides and LOLA terrain, runs in the browser, and is checked against JPL Horizons, with our limits stated openly.
details:
This is our response to the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge: an intuitive tool for mission planners, educators and the public to compare south-pole landing sites and dates, showing the Sun and Earth relative to the horizon to judge power and direct-to-Earth communication.

What it does: Southlight answers the question every south-pole landing team asks: where and when can we land and still have power and a link home? Pick any date from 2026 to 2030. The Sun and Earth glide to their real positions around a textured Moon. Three sites from NASA's Artemis III candidate-region lists each get a Good, Risky or Poor verdict: Malapert Massif and Nobile Rim 1 (on the 2022 and 2024 lists) and Connecting Ridge (on the 2022 list). The verdict card shows sunlight %, the longest dark stretch, Earth-in-view % and the longest gap without Earth. It works for a window of 7, 14 or 30 days, one lunar day (29.5 days) or one year. A line under each site gives its operable days (Sun and Earth both in view for at least half the day) and when its first dark stretch of 48 hours or more starts. A Nearest PSR readout gives the distance to the closest permanently shadowed region, a possible water-ice target.

How it works: Sun and Earth directions come from NASA NAIF DE440/SPICE kernels, interpolated in the browser. Each site's skyline is built from NASA GSFC LOLA south-pole terrain (40 m map, with an 80 m sensitivity check). The Sun and Earth are treated as discs, so partial rises and sets count. The window is stepped every 30 minutes. A best-window search checks every daily start over the next 365 days for the chosen window length and ranks windows by time with the Sun and Earth both in view, then sunlight, then shorter darkness. Nearest PSR uses the LROC PSR Atlas, which lists every south-pole permanently shadowed region of 10 km² or more, built on the LOLA illumination modelling of Mazarico et al. (2011). It is measured as the great-circle distance to each region's centre.

What you can explore: a shared Sun/Earth timeline linked to the Moon scene, a skyline chart that shows whether terrain or a lunar eclipse causes each interruption, and a 3D terrain close-up lit from the real Sun direction. A side-by-side table compares every site for the same window, with a calendar heatmap of every site by day. A "Find a better window" mission keeps the original and recommended windows side by side. "Play a lunar month" animates a full month of light around the pole. There are also shareable links and CSV export.

Benefits and impact: choosing a landing site and date normally takes specialist tools. Southlight gives a mission planner a verdict in one view, gives a teacher a way to show why the poles are hard, and lets anyone explore the real geometry. Planner, Educator and Public views present the same engine at three levels of detail, and shareable links and CSV export let results travel.

Trust, limits and what we considered: a "How we know" panel shows our checks against NASA/JPL Horizons, reference tests, the terrain-resolution comparison, the data sources and the limits. Our Sun and Earth directions agree with NASA/JPL Horizons within 0.0001 degrees at 3 sites on 3 dates. We compared a full year against a published JPL study as a neighbourhood check, not a match, and did not adjust anything to bring the numbers closer. Finer terrain can move a site's sunlight share by more than ten points. Verdicts held for our reference window but change in some 2027 windows, and the app flags those as terrain-sensitive. Earth visibility is geometric line of sight, not guaranteed radio service. Sunlight is not solar-array yield. Slopes, hazards and thermal conditions are not assessed. Nearest PSR is measured to a region's centre, and nearness indicates possible water ice, not confirmed ice. Good/Risky/Poor and the operable-day rule are our own definitions, not NASA standards, and we set the verdict thresholds before comparing anything with published values. We chose three sites so each verdict could be checked, used the 40 m terrain with an 80 m sensitivity check, and treated the Sun and Earth as discs.

Tools: TypeScript, React, three.js (WebGL), zustand and Vite in the browser, with Vitest tests against SPICE reference values. Python (SpiceyPy, NumPy, Rasterio, Pillow) prepares the data once. Everything runs client-side, with no server, account or API key. Hosted on Vercel.

Creativity: the pretty picture is the correct picture. The Moon's lit side, the glow and every pin colour are driven by the same engine as the numbers, and date changes animate the real orbital paths rather than faking a straight-line slide.

AI use and prior work: The team chose the challenge, set the goals and design, and directed the work. Claude (Anthropic, via Claude Code) and Codex (OpenAI) generated and revised substantial portions of the code, tests, documentation and data scripts, and helped with debugging, research and review. The displayed numbers are deterministic calculations from NASA data, not AI predictions. The demo video's voiceover is AI-generated with ElevenLabs text-to-speech; the footage is a screen recording of the live app. The sky shader, palette and visual style were created by our team and adapted from Voca, an earlier project of ours.

Try it out: https://southlight-tau.vercel.app
